documents.title: Why remote towns are betting on dark skies
documents.text:
A growing number of remote communities, short of other sources of income, are discovering that the night sky is an asset. In the highlands of the north, a village of four hundred people has seen its winter occupancy at local guesthouses rise by half since it received an international designation as a dark-sky reserve, a title awarded to places with exceptionally little artificial light.

The designation carries obligations. Residents agreed to replace streetlights with shielded fittings that direct light downward, and to turn off the lamps at the sports ground after ten o'clock. Not everyone was enthusiastic: some elderly residents worried about safety on icy paths, and a few businesses objected to dimmer signs. The council responded by installing low-level path lighting with amber bulbs, which disturb the view of the stars far less than white light.

Astronomers point out that the benefit is not confined to tourism. Dark skies are valuable for research, and the village now hosts a small observatory run by a university. The researchers say that the same measures that keep the sky dark also reduce energy bills, a modest saving, but one that the council is happy to publicize.

The authorities warn that the strategy has limits. Only a handful of places can claim truly dark skies, and as more villages seek the title, visitors may become harder to attract.

questions.explanation: The article shows tourism, research and savings from dark-sky policies.

documents.title: Proposal to extend a pilot scheme
documents.text:
To: Executive Leadership Team
From: Amara Nwosu, Head of Customer Service
Subject: Proposal to extend the live-chat pilot

Dear colleagues,

I am writing to recommend that the live-chat pilot, which has run in the northern region since January, be extended to the whole company for a further six months before a final decision is made.

The results so far are encouraging but not conclusive. Customers who used chat resolved their problems in an average of nine minutes, compared with twenty-two by telephone, and the satisfaction score for chat was four points higher. On the other hand, the pilot has handled only eight percent of contacts, and the customers who chose it were younger and more comfortable with technology than the average. It is possible, therefore, that the result flatters the service.

An extension to the whole company would give us a broader sample and a better idea of whether chat can serve older customers, who currently account for a third of our calls. It would also allow us to measure the effect on the telephone team, whose workload fell during the pilot but whose staff have expressed concern about the future of their jobs.

The additional cost, mainly software licenses, would be about 40,000 dollars. I would be glad to present these figures in more detail at your meeting on 12 November.

Regards,
Amara Nwosu

To propose extending the trial widely
To ask for more telephone staff now
To report that the pilot fully succeeded
questions.explanation: She recommends extending the pilot company-wide for six months.

questions.explanation: Chat averaged nine minutes against twenty-two by telephone.

questions.explanation: The telephone staff have expressed concern about the future of their jobs.

documents.title: Notice: temporary changes to refuse collection
documents.text:
BROADMOOR DISTRICT COUNCIL — WASTE SERVICES NOTICE

Because of the planned closure of the Calder Road bridge from 4 March to 12 April, collection of household waste in the Elmfield and Harlow areas will follow a temporary timetable.

Collection vehicles cannot cross the bridge, and the only alternative route adds forty minutes to each round. To avoid delays, the council has decided that general waste will be collected every two weeks instead of weekly in the affected areas during the closure. Recycling collection will continue weekly, as it requires a smaller vehicle that is able to use the Mill Lane crossing. Garden waste collection will be suspended entirely until 12 April, and the annual subscription will be extended by six weeks at no charge.

Residents may take additional household waste to the recycling center on Tanner Street, which will open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily during the closure. Households with babies in nappies, or with medical needs that produce additional waste, may apply for a weekly collection by calling the number below before 28 February.

We apologize for any inconvenience and thank residents for their cooperation. Collection days for each street are listed on the council's website and will also be posted on notice boards.

documents.title: Quality Assurance Manager, Hollis Foods
documents.text:
Hollis Foods, a family-owned producer of frozen meals supplying supermarkets across the region, is seeking a Quality Assurance Manager to lead its three-person quality team at the Rotherby plant.

The role carries responsibility for ensuring that every product leaving the factory complies with food-safety law and with the specifications of our retail customers. You will manage the system of inspections and audits, investigate complaints and, when something goes wrong, lead the response, which may include recalling products. You will also act as the contact for external auditors and for the local authority's inspectors.

The ideal candidate will have a degree in food science or a related subject and at least six years' experience in food manufacturing, of which at least two should be in a supervisory role. A thorough knowledge of the hazard-analysis system that underpins the industry is essential. We value, however, the ability to speak plainly to production staff over a collection of certificates, since the quality manager's greatest influence comes from persuading people to follow procedures even when under pressure to produce more.

We offer a salary of 52,000 to 58,000 dollars, depending on experience, and a bonus linked to audit results. The position requires flexibility, as occasional weekend work may be needed during peak periods. Applications should be sent by 10 October, and interviews will include a short exercise in analyzing a complaint.

documents.title: Letter requesting permission to use a photograph
documents.text:
Dear Mr. Lindholm,

I am writing on behalf of the Harborview Historical Society, which is preparing an illustrated history of the town's fishing industry to be published next spring. In the course of our research, we discovered a photograph of the harbor in 1952, taken by your late father, that appears in a family album you generously lent us last year for scanning.

We should like very much to include it in the book, on a full page, as the image shows with unusual clarity the arrangement of the old quay before it was demolished. I understand that the photograph remains in your family's ownership, and we would not wish to reproduce it without your permission. Should you agree, we would credit your father as the photographer and acknowledge the family in the preface.

I must be frank about the terms. The Society is a small charity, and we cannot pay a fee, although we will provide ten free copies of the book and the use of a high-quality scan for your own purposes. If you prefer, we would also be willing to include a short note about your father's career, which, we are told, spanned forty years.

I would be grateful for your decision by 15 January, so that we can finalize the layout.

Yours sincerely,
Henrietta Cole, Editor

documents.title: The case for teaching statistics earlier
documents.text:
Most school pupils learn to differentiate a polynomial long before they learn to interpret a poll. A growing number of educators now argue that this order of priorities is mistaken, and that statistics, not calculus, should form the core of the mathematics that every citizen learns.

Their case rests on how adults actually use numbers. Few will ever need to solve a differential equation, but nearly all will meet claims about risks, averages and probabilities, in the news, in medical advice and in financial products, and many will be unable to judge them. A study in which graduates were asked to interpret the results of a screening test found that a majority gave the wrong answer, even though the arithmetic involved was elementary.

Opponents of reform worry that the change would weaken preparation for engineering and physics, which depend on calculus. Supporters reply that it need not be an either-or choice: a school could offer a core of statistical reasoning for all pupils, with calculus as an option for those who intend to pursue science.

The difficulty is partly practical. Teachers who were themselves trained in traditional mathematics are not always confident with statistics, and a new curriculum would need a long period of preparation. Several regions that have tried it report that the effort has been worthwhile, though they concede it has taken longer than planned.

choices: Calculus should vanish from every school

questions.explanation: Educators argue statistics should form the core of everyday mathematics.

questions.prompt: What did the study of graduates show?
choices: Most had never learned any calculus

Few could calculate simple averages
All preferred polls to real tests
questions.explanation: A majority gave the wrong answer though the arithmetic was elementary.

questions.prompt: What compromise do supporters propose?
choices: A ban on calculus before university

A statistics core with optional calculus
A single course combining both subjects
questions.explanation: A core of statistical reasoning for all, with calculus optional for science.

questions.prompt: What does the last paragraph imply about reform?
choices: It requires patient teacher training

It is unpopular with most students
questions.explanation: A new curriculum needs long preparation; regions report it took longer than planned.

documents.title: A museum's new wing: ambitious but cold
documents.text:
The opening of the new wing at the Calloway Museum has been greeted with the kind of acclaim usually reserved for events in the capital. Designed by a Danish firm and clad in pale stone, the building is undeniably handsome, and its long gallery, lit entirely from above, makes the museum's collection of northern landscapes look finer than ever.

What the architecture achieves in the way of grandeur, however, it loses in warmth. Visitors are channeled through a sequence of high, silent rooms in which even a conversation seems an intrusion, and the benches, designed more for the eye than the body, discourage lingering. In the galleries devoted to local history, the objects are displayed in glass cases so large and so brightly lit that they seem like exhibits in a laboratory.

Some features are thoughtful. A small room at the end of the building offers a quiet view over the river and, unlike the rest, invites one to sit. The children's section, though modest, is intelligently arranged at a height that children can reach.

The museum has plainly spent its funds on the container rather than the contents, and one hopes that the next stage will provide the explanations and context that the displays currently lack. For now, it is a building to admire rather than to enjoy.

questions.explanation: It is handsome and grand but cold.

documents.title: Reminder on the use of personal devices
documents.text:
MEMORANDUM
To: All staff
From: Marcus Oyelaran, Head of IT Security
Subject: Use of personal devices for work email

Over the past six months, our security team has recorded an increase in the number of staff accessing company email on personal telephones and tablets. This is permitted, and I do not wish to discourage it, since many of you find it convenient. I am writing, however, to remind you of the conditions that apply.

Any personal device used to access work email must be protected by a passcode of at least six digits and must have the company's security software installed. The software allows us to erase work data remotely if the device is lost, but it does not affect your personal photographs or messages, a point that several colleagues have asked about. Devices that are more than four years old, or that have not been updated in the last six months, may not be used, since they are unable to receive security patches.

I should add that two devices were reported missing last quarter, and in one case the owner delayed reporting the loss for a week. A delay of this kind greatly increases the risk, and I ask all staff to report a lost device to the help desk at once.

An online guide to installing the software is available on the intranet.

documents.title: Hartley & Moss: independent financial planning
documents.text:
Money is the most common cause of anxiety in family life, and the advice that most people receive about it comes from institutions that profit from the products they recommend. At Hartley & Moss, we have arranged our business differently.

We charge a fixed annual fee, agreed in advance, and we accept no commission from any bank, insurer or investment provider. This means that when we recommend a pension, a savings plan or an insurance policy, we have no reason to prefer one over another except the interests of our clients. We tell prospective clients plainly that this will cost them money at the outset, and we invite them to compare our fee with the commissions that conventional advisers collect in the course of a decade.

Our first meeting is free and lasts an hour. During it we ask about your circumstances, your aims and your attitude to risk, and we explain how we would approach your situation. There is no obligation to continue, and we will not follow you with telephone calls.

We do not claim to offer higher returns; no honest adviser can. What we offer is advice that is independent and transparent, and the confidence that comes from knowing exactly who is paying us.

To arrange a meeting, call our office or complete the form on our website.
